title: Launch HN: Axonnic (YC F26) – Sleeves that track fingers and estimate force
summary: Hi HN! We’re Arsh and Max, founders of Axonnic ( https://axonnic.com ). We’ve developed a forearm sleeve that reads muscle activity to decode finger movements and estimate fingertip force, while leaving the hands bare. It’s used to record human movement and generate training data for dextrous robots. Here’s a demo video: https://youtube.com/shorts/xBrocTc9cfA We’ve found that electromyography (EMG) is a much better way to train robots than by video alone because video only captures movement, not muscle activity or the effort behind the movement. A useful signal can be present even when the hand barely moves; just maintaining a grip involves muscle activation. The subtle muscle movements that can barely be picked up in video are the most important details for activities like sewing and delicate assembly. The sleeve has 64 channels of surface electromyography, or EMG. Electrodes on the skin detect electrical activity from muscles in the forearm. We distribute sensors across the forearm so as to not overfit to one muscle group. We synchronize EMG with hand tracking to train a model that predicts finger joint angles, then we run the decoder solely from EMG, adding in fingertip force estimates that have been calibrated from finger presses on force sensors. When the user takes the sleeve off then puts it back on again, the electrode positions change, so we run tests over separate wearings. In one case, we ran a 215-second recording, four days after training, without any recalibration, and compared the results with Apple Vision Pro hand tracking. The result was just 6.9° error across 20 joint angles. We’ve published the measurements and evaluation details here: https://axonnic.com/benchmarks . We faced many challenges doing recordings in factories, including wireless interference and unreliable off-the-shelf hardware. This led to some bad recordings and the need to repeat data collection. For that reason, we’re developing our own electronics that use a wired PCB design that will eliminate interference and timing inconsistencies. Axonnic grew out of Max's EMG research at Oxford. We looked at using the technology for computer control, then we thought a more promising use-case was in capturing the effort involved in skilled manual tasks. This technology could be described as a computer to human interface. Where computers gain insight and learn from human skills. Sewing particularly stood out because the material deforms and the operator is constantly adjusting grip and tension. Maxim has an Oxford MBiol and conducted research on high-density surface EMG. He previously built internal tools at Skyscanner and worked at Voxblock across PCB development and supply chain. Arsh studied medicine at Oxford and has research experience applying machine learning to medical imaging, alongside software and robotics projects. Together we have built the sleeve, decoding software and data-collection system and tested them in industrial settings. So far we have the tech being used to record sewing and other manual tasks at a European manufacturer, which signed an LOI for support with robotic implementation. We have also collected construction demonstrations involving electricians, plumbers and demolition work. These are pilot and data-collection examples. Separately, our public demos include controlling a Proception robotic hand from forearm EMG. If you’ve done any of your own trials for training robots for manual tasks, we’d love to hear about what tasks you were trying to train for and how the trials went. We’re happy to discuss the hardware, calibration and models here in the comments. Thanks! https://axonnic.com Comments URL: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50522776 Points: 43 # Comments: 20

title: Launch HN: Onlook (YC W25) – An open-source developer tool for designers
summary: Hey HN, I'm Daniel, founder of Onlook ( https://github.com/onlook-dev/onlook and onlook.com). Onlook is a desktop app that puts a canvas on top of your real codebase, letting you design directly in code with the agent you already use. Over 25,000 designers and developers have supported the project, 100+ have contributed, and it's been the #1 trending repo in the world twice. We just rebuilt the entire product as an agentic design tool, and open-sourced it to the community. Here’s a demo video: ( https://youtu.be/BogcYWf4siM ) If you're an engineer, traditional engineering tools are largely built for convergence, whereas designers tend to explore and diverge on ideas. Onlook gives designers a familiar canvas while managing all of the dev processes that get between them and making mind-blowing designs in code. Designers can work on a multiple simultaneous worktrees that run on the real app locally, and every change lands as a PR you can review or throw away, so there aren’t mockups to rebuild. We built Onlook because we believe there needs to be a developer tool that works the way designers do. More and more, designers are expected to work in code. Designers think by seeing, drafting, arranging variations, using references, and remixing ideas. That’s why the canvas has been the signature feature of design tools because it genuinely is useful for how messy the creative process is. Most of the challenge of using engineering tools for design work is that the first half of starting a project often takes mental bandwidth in of itself (What branch am I on? What page was that last exploration on?) and the second half is constrained by configuring your coded design to present itself (prompting design tools on top of what you’ve built or making temporary navigation for that specific state). Some of you may remember our earlier Show HNs (July 2024: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=40904862 , August 2024: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=41390449 , May 2025: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=44127653 ). Since then, we built a web version (too early), then a Storybook-native build (a mistake). We noticed that our desktop product from July 2024 was still getting hundreds of downloads a month despite zero promotion, so we decided to rebuild it for the new era of designers working in code. How it works… Onlook shines at exploring tons of ideas at once. Ask it to lay out every flow in your product, show every state of a component, or riff on ten versions of one screen. Your designs all show up side by side on an infinite canvas, with each frame as a real webview running your actual app with real data. Not as a mockup, but the real deal. When we built this editor, we had an epiphany that it could be a new kind of IDE for design. Design tools used to be limited to a proprietary setup or closed schema, but now you can push and pull the medium of code to get whatever result you want, so why not give agents an infinite canvas of browsers and see what they do? It turns out, the agents can figure out how to better present coded work by adjusting the urls of browser frames and arranging and resizing them on the canvas. The concept is simple, but it requires a lot of product thinking. For example, because all of the frames on the canvas share a single browser session, and Chromium only allows six connections per host per session, ten frames of the same app end up fighting over limited connections. So, we had to plan around that, and there are still tons of things we need to do to make the canvas ultra performant. Onlook is an Electron app where you can import a repo from GitHub or upload a local folder. Then, Onlook creates a git worktree, starts your dev server, and has the agent sort out missing dependencies or other requirements. You never open a terminal and everything the agent does is a normal git diff that can go to GitHub as a PR. We inject a small script into each frame that draws selection outlines and reads the page, so that way you can click an element, say "make this a card layout," and the agent knows exactly what "this" is. This time we didn't build our own agent. Onlook runs Claude Code or Codex on your own subscription, and we turn whatever the agent emits into one typed event log and draw the UI from that in our own chat interface. On top of that we give the agent a bespoke set of design-specific tools, from arranging frames on the canvas, to making suggestions, to generating multiple iterations of a selection – which is especially useful because the agent decides how to get the app into a state that you need based on your prompt. We also have our own Artifacts which are quick HTML sketches that live in the editor, but outside your repo. They’re almost like components in other design tools in that they can be carried and edited across every project but are detached from the project with no network access. As an example, you can ask the agent to turn your interface into an Artifact, and use it as a reference for another exploration, or download it as HTML and send it to a coworker as an interactive export of something you have in progress. I frequently go back to the artifacts I’ve made as visual snippets when I need new ideas or need to borrow something that’s already been built. The desktop editor is free (you can download it from our website at onlook.com) and open source under Apache-2.0, and we'll eventually offer a paid cloud product for teams. We'd love to hear which repos work and which don't, what you try to do on the canvas, and what's missing. We’re so excited for this to be a new way for designers to work in code!
